anchors.paper_title: A large dataset of human EEG responses to short naturalistic videos for studying dynamic visual event processing
anchors.reason: Paper introduces the EEG Moments Dataset (EMD): 128-channel EEG and eye tracking from 6 participants viewing 1,102 videos, matching the dataset's authors and description.

metadata.methods_description: EEG and eye-tracking data were recorded while subjects viewed 3-second videos with audio over multiple sessions and runs, instructed to maintain central fixation. Raw data are in BIDS format, with preprocessed EEG, preprocessed eye-tracking and stimulus metadata provided as derivatives.

citation_details.title: A large dataset of human EEG responses to short naturalistic videos for studying dynamic visual event processing
citation_details.author: Alessandro T. Gifford, Pablo Oyarzo, Anne W. Zonneveld, Christina Sartzetaki, Iris I. A. Groen, Radoslaw Martin Cichy
citation_details.abstract: Vision neuroscience has experienced a surge in the collection and use of large-scale datasets of brain responses to naturalistic images. However, static images lack the temporal dimension essential for understanding how vision is solved in the brain during dynamic real life settings. To facilitate the study of the neural correlates of dynamic visual event perception, we introduce the EEG Moments Dataset (EMD). EMD consists of 128-channel EEG responses and eye-tracking recordings of 6 human participants viewing 1,102 short naturalistic videos (3-second long; with audio track) while maintaining central fixation. We show that EMD's EEG responses well encode stimulus-related information, exhibit a temporal correspondence with the video stimuli, and have a rich representational content revealed by brain encoding models based on different feature spaces. Furthermore, complemented by the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD) - an existing large-scale dataset of human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) responses for the same videos - EMD enables spatio-temporally resolved investigations of brain responses to dynamic visual events. We release EMD's EEG and eye-tracking data in both raw and preprocessed format, along with the 1,102 video stimuli, and rich stimulus metadata. Finally, we provide an interactive code tutorial to familiarize with EMD's preprocessed data, stimuli, and stimulus metadata.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
